text:
GRU4Rec represents interaction history through a recurrent hidden state used to score candidate items; aggregate shuffle sensitivity cannot identify which recurrent step loses useful information. [GRU4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06939) supplies the recommendation backbone, while [Theory of Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14823) shows how gates control memory timescales and context-dependent resetting in gated recurrent networks. This motivates examining update/reset gates and state changes by history lag, but gate saturation alone does not establish task-relevant forgetting.

[Zhang and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042) show that activation-patching conclusions depend materially on corruption methods and evaluation metrics. Proposed adaptation: construct paired original/perturbed training prefixes, hold the suffix, target and candidate set fixed, then restore original hidden states or gate activations at selected timesteps and replay the suffix. Measure changes in the fixed target–competitor score margin, m=s(target)−s(competitor), alongside hidden-state differences. Choose competitors before intervention; include identity patches, reverse patches and several bounded intervention strengths. Index lag using actual interactions and read out the final nonpadding position.

Interpretation remains conditional: an early state difference that disappears during replay suggests recurrent contraction; a persistent final-state difference with little margin change suggests insensitivity of the scoring pathway for those candidates. Local state/gate restoration that recovers the margin strengthens evidence for that computational location’s contribution, without proving a unique mechanism or generalization benefit. These are proposed GRU4Rec diagnostics extrapolated from gating theory and language-model patching research, not established GRU4Rec findings. Use the existing single trained model per category; training-prefix diagnostics require neither auxiliary predictors nor score fusion.
